title: Successive Percentages
tagline: Year 2 — Chains of percentage changes, net effect and the multiplier method

introduction.overview: When a quantity changes by one percentage and then by another, the second change applies to the new value, not the original. The net change is therefore found by multiplying the growth factors, not by adding the percentages. This single idea solves population growth, price changes, area changes of a rectangle, and consumption-versus-price problems.
introduction.placementRelevance: Successive percentage questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, either directly or inside area, profit, and population problems.
introduction.realWorldContext: Salary hikes in consecutive years, repeated price changes, and the effect of length and breadth changes on area use successive percentages.

learningObjectives: Use the multiplier method for two or more changes
Apply the formula a + b + ab/100 for the net change
Find the effect of changing length and breadth on the area of a rectangle
Reverse a series of changes to find the original value

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: An increase of r% multiplies by (1 + r/100) and a decrease of r% multiplies by (1 − r/100).

coreDefinitions: Successive percentage change: percentage changes applied one after another to the updated value.
Net change: final value compared with the original value, as a percentage.
Multiplier: the factor by which a value is multiplied for a given percentage change.
Area of a rectangle changes by the product of the multipliers of length and breadth.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Each percentage change is a multiplication. Two changes are two multiplications, and the order does not matter. The extra term ab/100 in the net formula is the "change on the change".
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Take the original value as 100. Apply each change in turn. 100 → +20% → 120 → +30% → 156. The net change is +56%.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Net change of two changes
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Use signs: increases positive, decreases negative.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Multiplier form
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Works for any number of changes.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Area of rectangle
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: l and b are percentage changes of length and breadth.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Price and consumption
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: To keep expenditure same after a price rise of r%.

mainNarrative: Convert each percentage to a multiplier and multiply. A rise of 20% followed by a rise of 30% is 1.2 × 1.3 = 1.56, a net rise of 56%. The formula a + b + ab/100 gives 20 + 30 + 6 = 56.
An increase of x% followed by a decrease of x% never returns the original. For x = 10: 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99, a net fall of 1%. In general the net change is −x²/100 %.
For a rectangle, the area is length × breadth, so the area multiplier is the product of the two multipliers. If length rises 10% and breadth rises 20%, area rises 1.1 × 1.2 = 1.32, i.e. 32%.
For price and consumption, expenditure = price × consumption. To keep expenditure the same after a 25% rise in price, consumption must be multiplied by 1/1.25 = 0.8, a 20% cut.
To reverse a chain, divide by the multipliers. If a value after +10% and +20% is 6,600, the original is 6600 ÷ 1.32 = 5,000.

deepDiveAspects.title: More than two changes
deepDiveAspects.content: The multiplier method scales to any number of steps: just multiply. The net formula is only convenient for two steps.

deepDiveAspects.title: Population and depreciation
deepDiveAspects.content: Population growing at fixed percentages is compound growth. A fall of 10% then a rise of 10% leaves 0.99 of the original.

solvedExamples.title: Two increases
solvedExamples.question: A number is increased by 20% and then the result by 30%. Find the net percentage increase.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The 30% applies to the already increased value.

solvedExamples.title: Area of a rectangle
solvedExamples.question: The length of a rectangle is increased by 10% and the breadth by 20%. By what percentage does the area increase?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The extra 2% comes from the product term 10 × 20/100.

solvedExamples.title: Price rise and consumption
solvedExamples.question: The price of sugar rises by 25%. By what percentage must a family reduce consumption to keep the expenditure the same?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: If price is 125% of the old, quantity must be 100/125 of the old.

shortcutMethods.title: Assume 100 and chain the changes

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Compute each change on the actual value.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Start with 100, apply each change and read the final number as the net percentage. Use a + b + ab/100 for two steps.

rulesForApplication: Divide by the multiplier to reverse a change.

commonMistakes.mistake: Wrong base for the second change
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Apply it to the new value.
Decrease is negative in the formula.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the same percentage to reverse

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: The net change of two increases must exceed their sum; use this to remove options.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: This topic is the foundation of compound interest.

summaryBullets: Price up r% → consumption down r/(100+r).

Can I find the area change for two percent changes?
Can I reverse a chain of changes?
